...New 00Z Aviation Discussion...

.KEY MESSAGES...
 
  - Scattered showers and thunderstorms are expected this
    afternoon and evening before widespread rainfall overspreads
    the area on Sunday.

 -  The potential for heavy rainfall and localized flash flooding
    peaks from Sunday into Monday with highest rainfall totals
    currently favored along and south of the I-85 corridor.

  - Temperatures trend more fall-like next week in the wake of a
    cold front.

&&

.SHORT TERM...
(This afternoon through Monday) Issued at 228 PM EDT Sat Oct 3 
2026

Showers got an early start this morning thanks to an unseasonably 
moist air mass in place across the southeast just ahead of a 
stalled frontal boundary across northern Georgia. The 12Z sounding
here in Peachtree City measured PWAT of 1.91" - just 0.02" short 
of the record for 12Z 10/3, though well short of the monthly 
record (October is still part of hurricane season, as we all have 
experienced in the past few years). This tropical air mass will 
linger through the rest of today and get reinforced into Sunday 
bringing the potential for some heavy rainfall to parts of north 
and central Georgia. 

Showers and a few rumbles of thunder will likely continue through 
the rest of the day. Temperatures may end up underachieving in many 
areas compared to the forecast thanks to the cloud cover and rain 
showers, but in places where the sun does come out it will be warm 
and moist with highs into the mid 80s. Isentropic analysis of the 
300K and 305K isentropes shows some shallow isentropic ascent is 
happening between 900-800mb which is in line with the vertical 
profile from this morning's sounding. As we heat up there is a bit 
of shallow instability in the low to mid-levels that is convectively 
enhancing some of the showers, leading to brief periods of heavier 
rainfall and the small chance of seeing a few rumbles of thunder 
where updrafts can get above the freezing level. Overall amounts 
shouldn't be anything of concern today in most places, but areas 
that experience repeated rounds of heavier rainfall could see an 
instance or two of flash flooding.

Looking at the broader synoptic picture, the trough over the 
northeast that brought the front in close to us pushes out over the 
Atlantic today. Surface high pressure sweeps in behind as DAVA and 
confluent flow aloft build in overhead. Surface high quickly pushes 
over the Appalachians and our favorite friend "the wedge" (CAD) 
moves southward into the CWA, pushing into the area tonight. Low 
clouds, showers of rain and some patchy fog are likely to great most 
folks across NE GA and the metro tomorrow morning. Alongside all 
this, a potent shortwave will dig towards the area, drawing up 
additional moisture from the gulf from a weak tropical wave. This 
system will progress across the CWA on Sunday. Isentropic lift will 
bring a steady rain to basically the entire CWA as moisture is 
lifted over the wedge and a southward progressing cold front. Some 
embedded convective elements will be possible, and the very high 
PWATs mean this rain could be pretty efficient at times. Basically, 
Sunday will probably be a wash out for most everyone. The upside is 
the temperatures will be much cooler than the previous few days - 
back into the 70s for most (and there is a chance some places in NE 
Georgia don't get out of the upper 60s). 

Several inches of additional rainfall will be possible on Sunday. 
Current hi-res ensemble guidance (both HREF and REFS) show average 
precip amounts of 1-3" for much of the area, possible a bit higher 
in south and east central Georgia. 90th percentile amounts likely 
represent an upper bound of some of the more convective elements, 
which shows some pockets of 4-5". These amounts are more likely 
along and south of I-85, where best moisture/lift look like they 
will coincide. These amounts don't quite warrant flood products. 
Places below the fall line have sandy soils that can handle quite a 
bit more rain than the more clay soils above, and rivers, creeks and 
streams are at the typical October minimums at the start of the 
"water year". That all said, heavy enough rain in the right place 
(like the urban jungle of Atlanta) can certainly trigger flash 
flooding, especially when an inch or two has already fallen over the 
past few hours.

Steady rain will continue through the afternoon and well into the 
evening hours for most. Rainfall should come to and end from 
northwest to southeast overnight for areas north of I-85 as the 
front begins to sag further south and drier air pushes in. This will 
be a slow process, so rain should linger well into the day on Monday 
for parts of central Georgia, and some showers may be possible as 
far north as the I-85 corridor depending on how the front stalls. 
Some clearing should begin Monday night for central Georgia, though 
again, uncertainty on how far south the front sags mean that showers 
could linger even into Tuesday.

&&

.LONG TERM...
(Tuesday morning through next Friday) Issued at 228 PM EDT Sat 
Oct 3 2026

The front lingers across far southern Georgia Tuesday and Wednesday. 
There is some uncertainty as to how much rain the very southern 
counties of our CWA will get as we move into next week. Forecast 
totals range from a half an inch to an additional two inches until 
the front is pushed off to the east on Wednesday. 

For a majority of the area however, rain is expected to come to an 
end overnight Tuesday morning. Dry air will settle in across much of 
the area north of a line from Columbus to Augusta with high 
temperatures in the mid to upper 70s. Overnight lows will fall into 
the 50s with 40's likely in the higher elevations of northern 
Georgia. By the time we get to Thursday, rain chances for the CWA 
drop to nearly zero. 

Long term models indicate that we'll be going into a weekly pattern 
as another short wave gets set to move through the upper level flow 
by next weekend which should bring showers and maybe a thunderstorm 
back into the forecast. &&

.SHORT TERM...
(Tonight through Sunday night)
Issued at 111 PM CDT Sat Oct 3 2026

A moist airmass remains concentrated across the area with PWATs 
ranging from 1.6 out west to around 2.2 inches to the east. While 
the front has become ill defined at this point, a mid-level shear 
axis remains across the Concho Valley into the Hill Country. This 
has helped to generate rain activity overnight into this morning 
with a few heavier pockets from Llano into Mason Counties. In the 
past few hours, this activity has decreased and lifted northward 
into the San Angelo and Fort Worth CWAs. The focus for any spotty 
activity looks to then shift east of the I-35 corridor over the 
Coastal Plains for this afternoon where enough breaks within the 
cloud cover could allow for limited enough instability with the 
limited daytime heating to help generate activity. Any heavier 
activity may produce some lightning and a quick half inch or more 
with brief downpours. This activity looks to fade this evening 
beyond sunset. However, overnight tonight into Sunday morning, is 
forecast to see possible reformation of scattered light, perhaps 
occasionally moderate, showers along that mid-level shear axis 
mostly focused across the Hill Country. This activity then fades 
going later into the day, especially into and through Sunday 
afternoon. Drier air then starts to work into the region from the 
north from Sunday night into Monday and will provide a pleasant 
weather forecast for the start of the long term period. Local 
temperatures hold in the 70s and 80s this weekend with light to 
moderate north-northeasterly winds and generally more clouds than 
sun.

&&

.LONG TERM...
(Monday through next Saturday)
Issued at 111 PM CDT Sat Oct 3 2026

Drier air advances southward into the region for early to midweek 
with a northerly flow generally in place across the low to mid-
levels of the atmosphere. Monday may still have enough lingering 
moisture for some cloudiness and a stray shower in the Edwards 
Plateau, otherwise rain chances come to an end with sunshine 
becoming far more prevalent. This drier air will result in a more 
refreshing airmass and feel featuring cooler mornings and mild 
afternoons with low humidity. The afternoon highs stay in the 80s 
for the most part while the morning lows dip down as low as the 
upper 50s across the Hill Country and into the low to mid 60s 
elsewhere.

Low rain chances (~15-20%) enter the forecast late this week into 
next weekend but the overall forecast confidence is lower than 
average for this time range as the latest guidance diverges 
regarding the possible evolution and also interaction between a 
weakness within the mid-level flow that may establish across the 
state and a possible disturbance associated with the Central 
American Gyre in the Bay of Campeche. Temperatures should remain 
seasonable in the morning but do slowly climb from midweek and 
afternoon highs will be warm with several nearing or reaching
the 90 degree mark.

.DISCUSSION...
KEY MESSAGE 1...Beautiful and refreshing fall weather continues into 
Sunday, though clouds increase during the afternoon. Showers arrive 
late Sunday afternoon/evening and become widespread Sunday night, 
potentially lingering into the Monday morning commute.

WOW. B-E-A-U-tiful conditions this afternoon! A true fall airmass 
has settled over southern New England, and what a notable difference 
from the lower 80s and dewpoints in the 60s yesterday afternoon. 
Refreshing! 925mb temperatures have settled around +10C, resulting 
in highs in the 60s this afternoon along with dewpoints in the 40s. 
For tonight, high pressure remains in control with mainly clear 
skies. Winds do not fully decouple, though still expect some 
radiational cooling with lows dipping well into the 40s. Not out of 
the question for a few upper 30s across the Berkshires.

High pressure transits northern New England on Sunday, leading to 
another quiet start to the day. Clouds will thicken from southwest 
to northeast by early afternoon ahead of a weak surface low 
developing off the Mid-Atlantic coast. Temperatures aloft are a 
touch cooler, with 925mb temperatures around +8C. Thus, expect highs 
a few degrees cooler than this afternoon, generally in the lower 
60s, with more clouds than sun during the afternoon. Sunday is not a 
washout. Based on the 12z suite of CAMs, showers could arrive as 
early as 3-5 PM, especially across western and southern portions of 
the region. However, the better chance for more widespread rainfall 
comes after 7 PM and continues through the overnight into early 
Monday morning.

Highest confidence in appreciable rainfall is across areas closest 
to the south coast, Cape Cod and Islands. Heavy rainfall is 
unlikely, as most convective elements should remain well south of 
Nantucket overnight Sunday into Monday morning. That being said, 
cannot rule out embedded thunder with showers south of Nantucket. 
The HREF does pick up on this potential, though probabilities remain 
low at less than 20 percent. How much rainfall? Generally a few 
hundredths to around a tenth of an inch for many, with totals of one 
to two tenths favored south of Route 44. Amounts could approach a 
quarter of an inch across Nantucket.

Rain should begin wrapping up during the Monday morning hours, 
though timing could result in a wet ride to school and work for at 
least portions of southern New England. Otherwise, no significant 
wind concerns with this system as easterly winds develop while the 
weak low passes nearby Sunday night.

KEY MESSAGE 2...Sharp temperature drop expected for the start of the 
week, then a return to dry, fall-like conditions with seasonable 
temperatures.

A deep Canadian low to our north tracks eastward heading into 
the start of next week with strong high pressure tracking just 
behind it, building in over the start of the week. Associated 
with this deep low, much cooler air is injected in across New 
England. 12z guidance continued to flirt with the possibility of
bringing the 540dam line closer to southern New England, but at
this time, it generally remains across Maine and New Hampshire 
with the latest run. 925 mb temperatures early Tuesday 
morning/late Monday night may sink to around 0C, then only climb
to around 5C in the afternoon hours Tuesday into Tuesday night.
This profile will be more supportive of highs barely making it 
to 60F and lows dipping into the 30s, especially Tuesday night 
with this cold air and diminishing winds.

The low continues eastward and the flow aloft then shifts more SW 
behind it, extending through the lower levels as well. High pressure 
at the surface exits towards Thursday with another high just behind 
it building in towards the Great Lakes. With the return of SW flow 
and drier conditions, more seasonable temperatures take hold for the 
back half of the week; 925 mb temperatures climb back to around 10C, 
supporting highs generally in the 60s, approaching 70F towards 
Thursday and Friday.

.DISCUSSION...
Issued at 1251 PM CDT Sat Oct 3 2026

The sun is shining and a look out the window (and most area 
webcams) show the sky with a brilliant blue color. Temperatures
have climbed into the mid 60s under the sunshine with upper 60s
expected for the high temperature today. GOES satellite water 
vapor imagery shows an amplifying wave over the eastern Dakotas 
and west-central Minnesota presently. Showers and isolated 
storms accompany the reflected surface front with the wave and 
are expected to track east through the overnight. The forecast 
leaned on the HRRR/RAP solutions (as they are doing a pretty 
good job at current conditions in the northern Plains) which 
keeps most, if not all, of the precipitation in Wisconsin 
tonight. A sliver of slight chance PoPs were kept in the 
northern tier counties just south of the Wisconsin state line, 
but given the amount of dry air over Illinois, confidence is
higher in just a few sprinkles compared to a wetting rain.  
Soundings show lapse rates aloft that are not terrible 
overnight, but instability should weaken as the system crosses 
the Mississippi River keeping the risk for lightning at bay. The
system should mostly pass over harmlessly, switching southeast 
winds to the northwest behind the front and ushering in a 
cooler, drier air mass.

Any mid-level cloud cover that moves over northern Illinois 
tonight with the system should help quell any localized shallow 
fog chances tomorrow morning. As winds turn to the northwest, 
temperatures will fall into the low 40s. Given the northerly 
flow expected tomorrow, high temperatures were nudged down 
slightly, but with cloud cover decreasing through the day, 
temperatures should once again return to the upper 60s with 
areas along and south of I-88 reaching the low 70s. Clearer 
skies are expected tomorrow night which will help drop 
temperatures back down to the low 40s with rural areas having a 
better chance at touching the upper 30s.

Seasonable temperatures will prevail through the week. High pressure 
will help maintain mostly drier conditions, although another 
wave over the northern Plains heading to Wisconsin mid-week 
will be monitored. Guidance continues to favor the track of the 
system north of Illinois so, for now, no precipitation is in the
foreseeable future. 

DK

&&

.AVIATION /00Z TAFS THROUGH 06Z MONDAY/...
Issued at 612 PM CDT Sat Oct 3 2026

Over the next 12 hours, a vigorous upper-level shortwave and 
associated surface low are expected to move across the Upper 
Great Lakes. As the system moves through, generally light (10kt
or below) south to southeast winds will gradually turn 
southwesterly through the night. Mid-level isentropic ascent 
will support bands of mid-level clouds and perhaps a few 
sprinkles through the night as well. 

After daybreak, a cold front will move through the terminals
turning winds west northwesterly. Efficient mixing will afford 
occasional gusts of 15 to 20 kt during daylight hours. Wind 
magnitudes will subside quickly after sunset as decoupling 
commences and the center of a surface high pressure system 
approaches from the west. Winds at ORD/MDW may trend westerly 
by the end of the 30-hour TAF window owing to the development of
a land breeze, but will keep a mention out for now given 
limited expected impact to aviation services. 

Borchardt

.SHORT TERM...
(This evening through Sunday)
Issued at 155 PM CDT Sat Oct 3 2026

Water vapor imagery early this afternoon provides a good look at 
the upper-level circulation responsible for our recent stretch of 
wet weather. The circulation is gradually shifting east across the
Southern Plains, with a plume of deep moisture wrapping around 
its eastern flank while notably drier air is already wrapping into
West Texas on its backside. This evolution is also becoming 
apparent on radar, where the more persistent rain has become 
focused across the eastern half of North and Central Texas while 
coverage continues to diminish farther west. Rain chances have 
therefore been adjusted from the NBM to better match current radar
trends and the expected eastward progression of the system.

The eastern and southeastern portions of the area will remain 
within a very moist column through the remainder of the afternoon,
so pockets of moderate to occasionally heavy rain will remain 
possible despite very limited instability. This will be more of a 
rainfall-efficiency problem than a convective one, with a deeply 
saturated atmosphere capable of producing locally high rain rates 
beneath the stronger echoes. This is most noteworthy across 
portions of Central Texas that have received considerable rainfall
recently, where additional heavy downpours could result in 
localized runoff issues. Otherwise, the progressive nature of the 
upper system and decreasing precipitation coverage should keep the
flooding threat localized. Extensive cloud cover and rain will 
continue to hold temperatures mainly in the 70s to near 80 this 
afternoon.

The transition to drier weather will accelerate on Sunday as the 
upper circulation moves east and the reservoir of much drier air 
currently over West Texas spreads into the region on northerly 
flow. Rain should steadily end from northwest to southeast around 
or just after daybreak Sunday, although a few showers may linger 
into Sunday afternoon across the eastern and southeastern counties
where deeper moisture will be slower to depart. Increasing 
subsidence and continued dry-air advection will then allow clouds 
to gradually clear through the day Sunday. The return of sunshine 
will support a warmer afternoon despite continued northerly flow, 
with highs ranging from the upper 70s to mid 80s.

&&

.LONG TERM...
(Sunday night through next Friday)
Issued at 155 PM CDT Sat Oct 3 2026

A quiet weather pattern will settle into North and Central Texas 
next week as the main belt of westerlies retreats well to our 
north and weak ridging becomes established across the Southern 
Plains. The substantially drier air arriving Sunday will remain in
place through much of the week, favoring mostly clear skies and a
fairly large diurnal temperature range. Overnight lows will 
generally fall into the 50s and lower 60s early in the week, 
followed by afternoon highs in the 80s. Gradually increasing 
heights and temperatures aloft will support a warming trend later 
in the week, with highs reaching the upper 80s to lower 90s by 
Friday.

Forecast uncertainty begins to increase beyond the end of the
period as guidance continues to differ on the evolution of
tropical moisture to our south. There is presently no clear
mechanism to bring that moisture far enough north to affect North
and Central Texas through Friday, so the dry forecast remains
favored. Trends in the western Gulf and adjacent lower latitudes
will bear watching heading into next weekend.

approaching 100 degrees for the central AZ deserts on Wednesday and 
Thursday. These will likely be the hottest days of the forecast

   upper 40s/50s; next weekend brings our next chance for rain.

.DISCUSSION...
Issued at 337 PM EDT Sat Oct 3 2026

It's a pleasant day across southern Indiana and north central 
Kentucky as the area of lower clouds has pushed southward into 
southern Kentucky. Temperatures have climbed into the upper 60s/low 
70s, with 7-12 mph northeasterly winds. While some lingering clouds 
could persist into tonight south of the Parkways, some clearing 
should allow more places in the southern ports of the CWA to 
experience some sunshine. 

For tonight and into tomorrow, a couple of features will skirt by 
the region before surface high pressure gets reinforced. A shortwave 
trough and associated weak surface cold front will swing over the 
Great lakes Region, grazing the far northern portions of the CWA. 
Another weak wave will pass through the Tennessee Valley, with both 
features exiting off to our east by Sunday evening. While the 
northern half of the area will contain fairly little moisture aloft, 
the northern periphery of a moisture field that extends south to the 
Gulf will provide enough moisture (1-1.5" PW) to allow for slight 
chances of rain showers early Sunday morning into early Sunday 
afternoon near the Lake Cumberland region. For places north, expect 
a dry and mostly sunny day with highs in the mid to upper 70s. Some 
patchy river valley fog is also possible tonight, especially for 
places that get calm winds and clear skies.

With surface high pressure being reinforced over the region 
beginning Sunday night, another stretch of dry and comfortable 
conditions will be in store. Weaker NNE flow will prevail through 
the early portions of the week, and with decent radiational cooling 
expected Monday and Tuesday night, temperatures will fall into the 
40s/low 50s. Recent guidance did hint at the potential for upper 30s 
lows Tuesday morning near the Bluegrass Region, but recent 
deterministic and ensemble guidance has trended away from this 
solution, shifting the area of coldest temperatures off to the north 
and east. Daytime temperatures will be close to normal for this time 
of year through Tuesday, with highs in the low to mid 70s along and 
north of I-64 and in the mid to upper 70s for places south.

The area of surface high pressure shifts to the east by Wednesday, 
allowing southerly flow to return to the region. Afternoon highs 
Wednesday and Thursday will be in the upper 70s/low 80s, increasing 
into the low to mid 80s by Friday and Saturday. Decent radiational 
cooling will keep temperatures on the cooler end, with lows in the 
upper 40s/low 50s forecast. Saturday morning temperatures will be 
slightly warmer, with lows in the low to mid 50s expected. While 
there is uncertainty on the arrival, our next chance for potential 
rainfall comes late Saturday into Sunday as a surge of tropical 
moisture pushes northward towards the region.

VFR conditions will prevail through this evening with clear skies 
and light south winds while surface high pressure moves into the New
England region. A low pressure system will quickly follow moving 
across the upper Midwest at this time with notable increase in mid to
high clouds and rainfall. Some of this rainfall along the tail end 
may reach MBS and FNT between 10Z to 12Z tomorrow morning. Only 
expect light rain if it does occur and ceilings anticipated to remain
VFR. Largely dry cold front passage through southeast Michigan on

.DTW THRESHOLD PROBABILITIES...

.PREV DISCUSSION...
Issued at 256 PM EDT Sat Oct 3 2026

DISCUSSION...

High pressure centered over northern lower MI has maintained a 
pleasant fall day across SE MI. East-northeast winds have wrapped 
enough lake moisture around the periphery of core subsidence to 
support a healthy coverage of diurnal cumulus over the 
southern/eastern portions of the area with sunny skies holding over 
the western/northern portions. Clouds fade early this evening with 
sunset leading to another cool night with lows falling into the 
lower 40s. 

A shortwave trough currently working across the upper Midwest tracks 
into the north-central Great Lakes late tonight as high pressure is 
shunted east. Moisture transport isn't particularly strong due to 
weak lower level winds (sub 40kts below 700mb), however is enough to 
draw in ribbon of modest theta-e from the Midwest along the lead 
edge of the mid-level wave/PV anomaly. Isentropic ascent is also 
confined along this lead edge resulting in a narrow band of 
potential showers sliding across between ~09-13Z. Owing to closer 
proximity to the shortwave and cold pool, said shower chances 
essentially confined north of I-69. Surface cold front lags, not 
crossing until Sunday evening, with minimal fanfare outside a low 
chance for an isolated shower/drizzle. 

Some of the coolest air of the season thus far follows as 850mb 
temps fall to 1-2C by Sunday night dropping lows to the low 40s-
upper 30s. Thermal troughing holds over the central Great Lakes 
through Monday as 850mb temps nudge down further to around 0C 
limiting diurnal recovery to highs near 60. Building surface high 
pressure late day Monday promotes clearing skies and near calm winds 
by Monday night supporting SE MI's first shot at frost, particularly 
across the Saginaw Valley/Thumb, as lows approach the mid 30s. More 
seasonably average temperatures return for the midweek period as 
Hudson Bay upper troughing shifts towards Labrador.

MARINE...

High pressure over the central and eastern Great Lakes region will 
gradually move over the Northeast through the end of the weekend as 
low pressure tracks east across southern Ontario, remaining north of 
Lake Superior. While this low is progged to remain well north of the 
area, it is expected to intensify as it moves east towards the James 
Bay area, resulting in a large-scale uptick in winds over the 
region. A cold front extending south from the low pressure system 
will also usher in a wind shift on Sunday. Tonight into Sunday 
morning, south winds prevail across Lake Huron. Winds then become 
westerly mid-day Sunday and gradually will shift and come out of the 
northwest Sunday afternoon and evening. Generally speaking Sunday 
through Monday, winds of 25 to 30 knots are expected over Lake 
Huron, with the strongest winds expected across the northern third. 
Sunday evening through Monday morning will see the best window of 
potential for winds around or in excess of 30 knots over the open 
waters of Lake Huron. This is especially so up across the far 
northern third of the lake. Will continue to monitor trends in the 
forecast and probabilistic data on low-end gale potential for Sunday 
night into Monday morning. Right now probability fields are around 
20% for seeing low-end gales around 34 knots across far northern 
Lake Huron. 

Further south on Lake St. Clair and the nearshore waters of Lake 
Erie, similar wind directions and wind shifts will be observed, but 
they will be delayed in time compared to over Lake Huron. Winds will 
also increase Sunday night into Monday; however, they will not be as 
strong that far south. 

Winds gradually weaken late Monday into Tuesday as a transient area 
of high pressure briefly moves through the region. We then see 
another system track north of the area, but will bring another 
uptick in winds for mid-week.
